full_text:
An ancient miser sold his houses, his vineyards, and his orchards, converting his entire earthly estate into a single, massive lump of solid gold. Fearing that thieves might rob him or servants cheat him, he carried the golden boulder into a secluded forest clearing and buried it secretly in a deep pit beneath an old willow tree.

Every afternoon, without fail, the miser walked to the lonely spot. He would dig up the soil with trembling fingers, gaze upon the cold yellow metal with ecstatic devotion, stroke its heavy surface, and bury it once more beneath the earth.

A watchful laborer, noticing the miser's daily pilgrimages and suspicious demeanor, trailed him to the woods. The moment the old man departed, the laborer dug into the loose dirt, unearthed the colossal nugget of gold, and carried it off to enjoy its fortune.

When the miser returned the next day and found an empty hole filled with scattered pebbles, he tore his garments, beat his chest, and wept with frantic lamentations that echoed through the hills.

A wise neighbor, hearing the wailing, ran to the clearing and asked what calamity had occurred.

"My gold! My life's treasure!" shrieked the miser. "I buried a giant lump of gold in this very spot, and a vile thief has stolen it away!"

"Did you ever spend any of it?" asked the neighbor. "Did you buy food, help your family, or purchase warm clothes?"

"Never!" cried the miser in horror. "I never touched a single grain of it; I came only to look upon it every afternoon!"

The neighbor picked up a heavy, jagged river stone, threw it into the pit, and said calmly: "Cover that stone with earth and come look at it every day! It will serve you precisely as well as your gold, for when you possessed the gold, you made no more use of it than you will of that rock."
moral: Wealth unused is no better than a common stone; possession without purpose is worthless.
